ORIGINAL RESEARCH article

Front. Environ. Sci., 04 November 2026

Sec. Water and Wastewater Management

Volume 14 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2026.1916894

Data-driven well-resolved aggregate-capacity screening for brackish-blending management in Kuwait under pumping and total-dissolved-solids constraints

  • FA

    Faisal Alshammari 1

  • MA

    Mosab Alrashed 2

  • AG

    Abdelaziz Gamil 3*

  • MA

    Mohamad Atyeh 4

  • 1. Engineering and Environmental Department, Ministry of Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy, Kuwait, Kuwait

  • 2. School of Engineering & Computing, American International University, Jahra, Kuwait

  • 3. Centre for Propulsion and Thermal Power Engineering, Cranfield University, Cranfield, United Kingdom

  • 4. College of Business, Australian University, Kuwait, Kuwait

Article metrics

View details

Abstract

Brackish groundwater is a strategic supply buffer for arid states reliant on energy-intensive seawater desalination, yet the operational condition of legacy well fields and the distribution-side limits on dispatchable volume remain understudied. Both are addressed here for Kuwait, where desalination supplies 92% of municipal water. A ministry-level record of 393 wells across five production fields was assembled, and a well-resolved screening linear program was formulated to maximize brackish blending subject to the 1,000-ppm upper total-dissolved-solids (TDS) limit of the applicable Gulf drinking-water standard and an aggregate pumping bound. The model resolves individual wells but represents the distribution side as a single aggregate capacity scalar; it is a screening model, not a hydraulic network model, and its optimum is an upper bound on what a station-resolved network could deliver. Current operations support 62.24MIGD of blending; all rehabilitation scenarios saturate the pumping bound at 90.70MIGD, a 1.46 (45.7%) uplift. The binding constraint is, therefore, distribution-side aggregate capacity, not upstream well availability. This finding is robust: a zone-partitioned re-solve yields 87.8 MIGD–90.70MIGD, and crediting the standby reserve shifts the binding constraint to the TDS limit; well availability never binds. Constraining dispatch to the nine documented pumping stations reduces the realizable volume to 55.08 MIGD (61% of the aggregate optimum) when each field feeds a single station, quantifying the cost of the full-connectivity assumption; the binding constraint stays on the distribution side in every case. A lexicographic formulation returns the same volume at lower delivered TDS, yielding a unique dispatch portfolio. The S0S3 transition increases the TDS-feasible substitution ceiling by 45.7% (a theoretical upper bound under cogeneration coupling), supporting SDG 6 targets 6.4 and 6.5. The TDS volumes reported represent TDS-feasible blending maximums for the distribution system and do not independently determine that the blended product will be safe for consumption. This diagnostic (i.e., comparing the rehabilitation well flow rates with the production flow rate of the existing firm distribution system) can also be applied to other arid-state utilities.

Highlights

  • Blending is limited by available distribution-system pumpage once mechanically failing wells have been returned to service.

  • Restoring mechanically failing wells increases potential brackish blending by 45.7% (62.2490.70 MIGD), after which additional well restoration does not increase the overall brackish blending volume but rather may improve the water quality.

  • The results were found to be robust: at no time did well availability become the limiting factor in this problem, regardless of whether standby pumps were included in calculations or if the distribution network was divided into separate zones.

  • A generalization applicable to all arid-state utilities is, therefore, to first compare firm distribution-system production flows against the total potential rehabilitation flows for individual wells prior to proceeding with investments in repairing wells.

  • The scope of this model includes resolving individual wells but aggregating them as one capacity on the distribution side. The model determines which end of the pipeline the constraint lies within; it does not simulate hydraulic behavior, and the optimum it reports is the upper limit of a station-resolved solution.

1 Introduction

Arid states have a compounded water security problem due to increasing population and increasing per capita demand, heat extremes associated with climate that exacerbate summer peak load conditions, and slowly degrading supporting infrastructure that may be operating beyond its designed lifetime (UNESCO, 2019; Ghaffour et al., 2013). Desalination accounts for over 90% of the municipal potable water in the Arabian Gulf (Fanack Water, 2024b; WaterHQ, 2021). Consequently, brackish (low-salinity) groundwater resources are generally under-evaluated. Brackish water is commonly mixed with desalted permeate at the distribution point to enhance mineral content, decrease corrosion potential, and, from an environmental perspective, extend the volume of water produced by high-energy thermal and membrane desalination processes (Ghaffour et al., 2013; Missimer and Maliva, 2018; Mukhopadhyay and Akber, 2018). Due to the mixing function associated with this application, brackish well fields are a low-profile but significant component of the water–energy nexus in arid municipalities.

Kuwait offers an exemplary case. The state has no perennial surface water bodies; natural water resources are limited to brackish groundwater stored in the Kuwait Group and Dammam Formation aquifers, with only small isolated freshwater lenses [1,000 mg/L total dissolved solids (TDS)] in the Raudhatain and Umm al-Aish depressions held as a strategic reserve (Fanack Water, 2024a; Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences, 2020). Desalinated water provides approximately 9% of domestic and industrial demand and roughly 60% of the total water supply (Fanack Water, 2024b); the per capita water use (165 ) is among the highest globally (Tariq et al., 2022). Brackish groundwater from the Shagaya, Salibiya, Umm Qudair, Wafra, and Atraf fields, with well-head salinities typically 3,000 mg/L–9,000 mg/L (Fanack Water, 2024a; Rashid et al., 2022), is already blended with desalinated water at salinities below approximately 5,000 ppm to produce potable supplies, irrigate agriculture, and serve non-potable industrial uses (Mukhopadhyay and Akber, 2018; Al-Ruwaih, 2010). The aggregate impact of legacy infrastructure deterioration on this blending capacity has not, however, been quantified in the peer-reviewed literature.

Our objective in this study is to provide that quantification through a linear-programming optimization that (i) encodes Kuwait’s brackish-well network at well resolution, (ii) couples per-well design and salinity attributes to the connected reservoir and pumping-station capacities, (iii) formulates and solves a blending optimization subject to a 1,000 ppm operational TDS and aggregate pumping-station capacity constraints, (iv) benchmarks the LP against a sorted-by-salinity greedy heuristic, and (v) maps the binding-constraint frontier with a sensitivity sweep over the pumping and TDS bounds. A polynomial salinity diagnostic with seed-stable cross-validation is retained as a feature-importance probe but is not used inside the LP because its modest out-of-sample accuracy is incompatible with the TDS-limit operational regime. The framing follows the Water and Wastewater Management section’s mission, and the study is positioned as a transparent, interpretable optimization-based decision-support approach that integrates hydrostratigraphic salinity structure, real infrastructure constraints, and a machine-learning salinity diagnostic for water management: a concrete water-management practice (which well, how much, and at what blending ratio, under real infrastructure constraints) is being optimized from operational data rather than simulated abstractly. A deliberate methodological choice, the exclusion of the machine-learning surrogate from the decision loop (Section 4.6) because a measured-salinity LP is safer than a surrogate-fed one once a hard quality limit governs, is itself reported as a result. Climate variability enters only as a boundary condition in scenario stress tests of the proposed blending strategy.

The article is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on brackish-water blending, well-field optimization, and data-driven approaches to multi-aquifer groundwater systems. Section 3 details the study area, hydrogeological setting, brackish-water quality and blending rationale, and the operational and historical datasets used. Section 4 formalizes the LP, the polynomial salinity diagnostic, the greedy baseline, and the sensitivity sweep. Section 5 reports the network description, the five-scenario analysis, the greedy benchmark, and the sensitivity frontier. Section 6 discusses the supply-security, energy, and SDG 6 implications, and Section 7 concludes.

2 Literature review

2.1 Brackish-water blending in desalination-dependent systems

Blending brackish groundwater with desalinated permeate is a long-standing practice in arid-zone municipal water supply, with documented operational and economic benefits in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and Spain (Ghaffour et al., 2013; Missimer and Maliva, 2018). Al-Ruwaih (2010) determined “the best ratio between distilled water and brackish ground water” for blending for drinking purposes; they showed that the selection of an appropriate blending ratio allows the production of drinking water that meets the drinking-water standards while reducing the amount of fully treated water produced, and their results provide both the practical and regulatory context for the constraints incorporated into the optimization problem in this study. On a broader scale, brackish-water reverse osmosis has been shown to be a significantly less energy-intensive process than desalination of seawater, and its cost and energy requirements are a function of the quality of the brackish-water input (Pearson et al., 2021). In the Gulf region, however, much of the brackish-water resource is non-renewable; therefore, when determining whether brackish water should be used as either a blending component or a feed for desalination, the implications of long-term depletion of the underlying aquifers must also be considered (Al-Zubari, 2003).

In terms of methodology, the closest precedent to the present work is Al-Zahrani and Ahmad (2004), who applied a stochastic goal programming (GP) model to determine daily production schedules for desalination plants located at water blending facilities in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia. At those blending facilities, desalinated water is blended with brackish groundwater drawn from several different well fields. Four main objectives were pursued in that GP model: (i) to satisfy customer demands, (ii) to maintain acceptable levels of salinity in the water being supplied, (iii) to avoid excessive depletion of the groundwater resources, and (iv) to maximize utilization of the available brackish water. These objectives have structural similarities to those of the present study. The primary differences are that (i) the earlier study solved its GP problem using stochastic techniques, whereas this study uses a deterministic LP, with demand being fixed at a single-scenario value of 520 MIGD; (ii) the earlier study represented the 1,000 ppm TDS threshold as a soft goal-deviation term, whereas this study represents that constraint as a hard linear inequality; and (iii) the earlier study did not couple the blending decision to an explicit distribution-side capacity scalar. The primary novelty claimed here is empirical rather than algorithmic: a 393-well, ministry-level census of asset condition (status, fault category, and root cause) paired with field-resolved salinity for a previously undocumented national brackish network, which the optimization then uses to localize the binding constraint. The optimization machinery itself is intentionally transparent (a deterministic LP rather than the stochastic goal program of Al-Zahrani and Ahmad, 2004, or the more general mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) formulations of Thomas and Sela, 2024; Housh, 2023), so that the binding constraint, not the solver, carries the planning message. No comparable well-resolution asset-and-blending analysis for Kuwait’s multi-field brackish network exists in the published literature. Table 1 contrasts the two formulations.

The present study contrasted with its nearest methodological precedent, the stochastic goal programming (GP) blending model of Al-Zahrani and Ahmad (2004).

The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) desalination sector provides the system-scale context for this blending strategy. Moossa et al. (2022) report a total GCC desalinated-water capacity of 97.2 MCM/d in 2020, accounting for approximately 40% of the global output, with an MSF-dominated but increasingly seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) fleet facing mounting energy and brine-disposal costs. This scale makes brackish blending a strategically significant demand-side lever: each MIGD of brackish water dispatched into the distribution system displaces one MIGD of seawater intake, reducing the brine outfall volume and desalination-plant throughput in proportion (Missimer and Maliva, 2018).

2.2 Hydrogeology and long-term hydrochemistry of Kuwait’s production fields

Long-term hydrogeochemical monitoring of Kuwait’s main brackish-water production fields (Rashid et al., 2022) documents progressive changes in groundwater chemistry, including increasing salinity and evolving major-ion composition over decades of pumping, which shows that extraction strategies must be coupled with quality-based constraints. AlAli (2008) provides a historical perspective on field development and abstraction over the period 1970–2008, classifying groundwater into fresh, slightly brackish, and brackish categories; together with the long-term hydrogeochemical record (Rashid et al., 2022), these works provide the conceptual hydrogeological backbone of the multi-aquifer system that is extended here with a well-resolved, aggregate-capacity linear-programming blending layer. The sustainability analysis of brackish abstraction from the Eocene aquifer in central Kuwait (Al-Eisa, 2020) provides a quantitative reference point for the upper bounds imposed on total extraction.

The Salibiya (Al-Sulaibiya) field, the oldest and largest brackish field in the present dataset (111 wells, 21.81 MIGD), has received dedicated hydrochemical study. Alhumoud et al. (2010) reported a per-well time-series (1991–2005) for the Dammam Formation carbonate aquifer at Al-Sulaibiya, documenting TDS in the range 3,523 mg/L–9,460 mg/L across monitored wells, with Na–Cl and Ca– hydrochemical facies. This field-specific range is consistent with the mean salinity of 4,805 ppm encoded in the LP for the Salibiya sub-network and confirms that the Ministry workbook values are physically realistic. The study also establishes that the Dammam Formation at this field is a confined-to-semi-confined carbonate aquifer with significant spatial heterogeneity in TDS, a result directly supporting the decision (Section 4.6) to use measured rather than surrogate-predicted salinity. Complementary geochemical tracing of Kuwait’s coastal groundwater documents the evolution of acidic hypersaline water along flow paths (Sabarathinam et al., 2020), reinforcing that well-head salinity is spatially heterogeneous and must be respected at field resolution rather than averaged away.

A current GCC-wide overview by Sherif et al. (2023) reports annual renewable desalination capacity of 26.4 billion across the six GCC states, average per capita consumption of 550 L , and persistently low treated-wastewater reuse fractions, confirming that the structural water-security gap motivating the present study is region-wide rather than Kuwait-specific. Beyond the Gulf, the mechanisms that govern groundwater-quality evolution (mineral dissolution, land-use forcing, and abstraction-driven enrichment) have been resolved in arid and semi-arid aquifers using integrated hydrogeochemical and geospatial methods (Jat Baloch et al., 2022a; b; Zhang et al., 2024), and contaminant fate-and-transport studies increasingly couple this geochemistry to explicit water-quality and health-risk assessment (Jat Baloch et al., 2025). These studies establish the field-resolved, geochemistry-aware treatment of groundwater quality that the present optimization operationalizes as a hard TDS constraint.

2.3 Well-field optimization

The optimization of pumping schedules across networked wells has been studied for decades, originally in the context of agricultural irrigation and more recently for municipal supply (Maier et al., 2019). Classical approaches (linear and dynamic programming and mixed-integer formulations) remain widely used but struggle to capture the non-linear interactions between aquifer drawdown, well-head salinity, pump efficiency, and downstream blending constraints. Recent work has begun to integrate data-driven surrogates into the optimization loop (Rajabi et al., 2015), exploiting the ability of statistical and machine-learning methods to approximate response functions from historical operational data without requiring full 3D groundwater flow simulation; the present study retains a polynomial surrogate only as a diagnostic and instead relies on the LP for the dispatch decision. Mathematical-programming formulations remain the workhorse for operational water-network decisions: Thomas and Sela (2024) developed a MILP framework for general water-network operations, and Housh (2023) used MILP approximations to optimize multi-source supply systems that explicitly include a seawater-desalination array, a setting structurally close to the brackish–desalinated blending problem treated here. For arid regions specifically, Kizhisseri et al. (2022) showed that mixed-integer optimization can serve as a decision-support tool for national water-sector planning and policy. These works motivate the choice of a transparent linear program (rather than a metaheuristic or black-box optimizer) so that the binding constraint remains directly interpretable for planning. The broader engineering-systems-optimization literature is methodologically aligned with the present analysis along three axes: uncertainty quantification and error estimation for numerical models (Alrashed et al., 2020) parallel the sensitivity sweep used here to bound the binding-constraint result; performance-indicator design for complex engineered systems (Alrashed et al., 2022) parallels the decision-relevant metrics through which the rehabilitation scenarios are compared; and stochastically optimal control under input uncertainty (Alrashed et al., 2026) frames the deterministic-versus-stochastic modeling choice that distinguishes the present LP from the stochastic goal program of Al-Zahrani and Ahmad (2004).

2.4 Machine learning in water resources

The water and wastewater management literature has seen rapid growth in machine-learning applications, including pipe-burst prediction, water-quality forecasting, and demand modeling (Liu et al., 2018). A highly active strand provides direct predictions of both groundwater salinity and total dissolved solids from measurable characteristics of wells (Tran et al., 2021; Elzain et al., 2024). Several machine-learning algorithms have been benchmarked for predicting salinity across a variety of multi-layered coastal aquifers (Tran et al., 2021), and optimized ensemble learning methods have been shown to predict levels of TDS in the groundwater of an arid coastal region (Elzain et al., 2024). These results are relevant here because they inform the development of the polynomial salinity diagnostic described in Section 4.6 and indicate the limitations of surrogate models under operating conditions constrained by a hard quality limit. In parallel, digital-twin and smart-water-grid concepts are being applied to expose how distribution-network topology and pumping constrain system efficiency (Ramos et al., 2023). The present study extends this line of work by applying a well-resolved, aggregate-capacity encoding of the brackish-well system to a desalination-blending objective while complementing the long-term hydrogeochemical record for Kuwait (Rashid et al., 2022; AlAli, 2008).

2.5 Water–energy nexus in desalination-dependent systems

Seawater desalination is energy-intensive, with multi-stage flash (MSF) plants requiring substantially more energy per than SWRO, and with GCC cogeneration coupling to thermal power blocks introducing additional constraints on dispatchability (Ghaffour et al., 2013). Kuwait’s fleet is historically MSF-heavy; Alotaibi et al. (2025) reported from first-principles energy and exergy analyses of actual operating data for Kuwait’s three main MSF plants (Al-Doha East, Al-Zour, and Al-Sobia) that the modern plants achieve 17%–21% lower energy and exergy consumption than their 1970s-vintage predecessors, with the fleet sitting toward the upper end of the regional MSF range. Section 6 applies these Kuwait-specific plant benchmarks together with the SWRO range from Ghaffour et al. (2013) to translate the S0S3 brackish-blending displacement into a quantitative energy and carbon footprint, subject to the cogeneration caveat discussed there. The tight coupling between water production and the power system in desalination-based sectors has itself become a focus of systems analysis: Salomons et al. (2023) showed that electricity load-shedding programs propagate directly into desalination output, illustrating why the displacement estimated here is best read as an upper bound that depends on dispatch flexibility.

Work published since 2021 has moved in three directions that bear directly on this study. First, blending has been treated increasingly as a formal optimization rather than a rule of thumb: Shalby et al. (2026) optimized blending ratios for brackish-groundwater desalination in Egypt’s Moghra aquifer so as to maximize the delivered quality while minimizing the desalinated volume required, which is structurally the dual of the objective used here. Second, the water-chemistry rationale for blending has been sharpened. Nativ et al. (2021) showed that desalinated brackish water requires deliberate mineral-composition management rather than simple dilution, and Lu (2023) provided computational methods for re-mineralization by blending; both bear on the observation (Section 4.5) that permeate at 50 ppm falls below the 100-ppm regulatory floor and must be blended or remineralized regardless of volumetric considerations. Third, the arid-state energy framing has been updated: Alenezi and Alabaiadly (2025) reviewed the emerging desalination technology landscape from a Kuwaiti perspective, and Elyaakouby and Tilioua (2026) optimized reverse-osmosis energy use in an arid North African setting, while Abdou et al. (2024) quantified the economic burden of water scarcity across the GCC. What none of these establishes, and what motivates the present study, is where the operational ceiling on blending lies in an existing national network whose assets have partly failed.

2.6 Knowledge gap

Four gaps motivate the present work. First, the operational condition of legacy brackish well fields in the Arabian Gulf is not systematically documented in the open literature at well resolution. Second, the consequences of that condition for the energy intensity of municipal desalination have not been quantified at the well-network resolution and linked to Kuwait-specific MSF plant benchmarks. Third, capacity-aware optimization frameworks that jointly model blending ratios, rehabilitation priorities, and distribution-side capacity constraints across multi-field, multi-aquifer systems are absent from the Kuwait literature; the closest analog (Al-Zahrani and Ahmad, 2004, for Saudi Arabia) does not resolve the pumping-station bottleneck or operate at well-field resolution. Fourth, the empirical identification of when distribution-side capacity binds before upstream well availability (a finding that determines whether investment should be sequenced as wells-first, pumping-first, or co-staged) has not been performed at well resolution for any GCC network in the published literature. In this study, we address all four gaps using a ministry-level dataset for Kuwait spanning 1970–2026.

The novelty claimed is, therefore, empirical and diagnostic rather than algorithmic, and it is worth stating precisely what is and is not new. The optimization machinery is deliberately ordinary: a deterministic linear program is chosen so that the binding constraint rather than the solver carries the planning message. What is new is (i) the asset layer, a well-resolved census of the operational status, fault category, and root cause for a national brackish network that has not previously been described in the peer-reviewed literature; (ii) the coupling of that asset layer to the documented distribution-side capacity schedule, which is what makes it possible to ask which side of the system binds; and (iii) the resulting diagnostic, that firm distribution throughput should be benchmarked against rehabilitated well capacity before well-repair investment is sequenced. Table 2 positions the study against the closest recent work on the parameters that govern transferability: water-scarcity context on two indicators drawn from a single common source so that the rows are comparable, the resolution at which assets are represented, and whether a distribution-side constraint is modeled at all. The scarcity columns make the Kuwaiti case explicit: renewable internal freshwater is effectively zero, so the withdrawal-to-internal-resource ratio is undefined rather than merely high, and every unit of municipal supply is manufactured or mined. These comparisons illustrate that recent optimizations of blending schemes address the chemical properties of the water and the economics of the plants involved effectively, but they do so without addressing the constraints associated with the distribution network, which is exactly what this study addresses.

The water-scarcity columns are national-context indicators taken from one common source so that rows are comparable (World Bank, 2026); they are not figures reported by each study. RIFR is renewable internal freshwater resources per capita (, 2021–2022); withdrawal is annual freshwater withdrawal as a percentage of internal renewable resources, which exceeds 100% wherever supply comes from desalination or trans-boundary inflow. Kuwait’s ratio is undefined because its internal renewable resource rounds to zero—the sharpest available statement of the scarcity that this study addresses: essentially no renewable internal water, against municipal consumption of (Tariq et al., 2022) and l across the GCC (Sherif et al., 2023). Process-scale and regional studies without a single national setting are marked “—”.

3 Study area and data

3.1 National water context

Kuwait is an extremely water-scarce country with no perennial surface water bodies; natural water resources are limited to brackish groundwater stored in the Kuwait Group and Dammam Formation aquifers (Fanack Water, 2024b; a). National water requirements are met primarily by three sources (seawater desalination, treated wastewater, and brackish groundwater), with desalinated water providing approximately 92% of domestic and industrial demand and approximately 60% of the total water supply (Fanack Water, 2024b; WaterHQ, 2021). Per capita water use is among the highest globally (165 ) (Tariq et al., 2022), and the country’s heavy dependence on energy-intensive coastal desalination plants is identified as a key vulnerability in long-term water security (Mukhopadhyay and Akber, 2018; UNESCO, 2019). The Water Action Hub places Kuwait’s brackish groundwater fields at a production capacity of order 545,000 (CEO Water Mandate/Water Action Hub, 2023).

3.2 Hydrogeological setting and well fields

This study addresses five of Kuwait’s largest brackish-water production areas feeding the national distribution system: Shagaya (sub-fields A–E, Al Jahra-Alabdliya structural province), Salibiya (Sulaibiya), Umm Qudair (Umm Gudair), Wafra, and Atraf. All five draw on the multi-layered clastic and carbonate aquifers of the Kuwait Group and on the underlying Dammam carbonate formation. The hydraulic and hydrochemical behavior of the Dammam carbonate aquifer in Kuwait, and its compatibility with injected desalinated water, are established in the primary literature (Sayed and Al-Ruwaih, 1995; Al-Ruwaih, 1995; Mukhopadhyay et al., 1998), and that work underpins both the horizon assignments and the blending rationale adopted here. Shagaya, Salibiya, and Umm Qudair are among the largest brackish-water producing fields in the country; each has had numerous production wells drilled to contribute to both municipal and agricultural demand (Rashid et al., 2022; AlAli, 2008). Studies examining hydrochemistry have found a decline in water quality due to increased salinity and changing ion composition caused by long-term pumping, so quality must be considered when developing strategies for water production (Rashid et al., 2022; AlAli, 2008). The Wafra area in southern Kuwait is one of the country’s principal agricultural zones, where brackish groundwater is abstracted intensively for irrigation; the Atraf field, located in western Kuwait, is a large brackish-water field with on the order of 80 production wells developed in the Kuwait Group aquifer that is increasingly used to support municipal and industrial demand (Al-Eisa, 2020).

The five Shagaya sub-fields were drilled between 1970 and 1972 to depths of approximately 1,150 ft–1,408 ft and draw on a mixed producing-horizon membership rather than a single clean horizon: of the 115 Shagaya wells, 69 are tagged to the Dammam carbonate and 46 to the dual horizon of the Kuwait Group (Table 3), with the dual-dominant sub-fields (A and E) being shallower-producing than the Dammam-dominant sub-fields (B, C, and D). Field labels are, therefore, operational/structural groupings, not one-to-one hydrostratigraphic units (see Section 5.2); their per-sub-field well counts, depths, salinities, and rated capacities are listed in Table 4.

The remaining four brackish fields span three further drilling cohorts and horizons. Salibiya (Sulaibiya; Sulaibya SW R1–R3 sections), the oldest and largest field, comprises 111 wells drilled during 1952–1956 in the shallow Dammam Formation (mean 871 ft); among the large fields, it is the most saline (4,805 ppm) and the principal rehabilitation target (AlAli, 2008; Rashid et al., 2022). Umm Qudair (Umm Gudair; lines A–C), the largest single field by rated capacity (50.75 MIGD), comprises 72 dual-horizon wells drilled during 1984–1986 (mean 1,092 ft, 3,829 ppm) (Rashid et al., 2022). Atraf (Jahra-A L.K/L.L sections) contributes 81 Kuwait Group (“KW”-horizon) wells drilled in 1990 (mean 690 ft, 4,593 ppm, 30.73 MIGD) (Al-Eisa, 2020). Wafra, in the southern agricultural zone, enters only as a small municipal sub-network (two wells, 5,000 ppm) that under-represents the field’s larger irrigation stock.

The Raudhatain lens (12 wells in the Dibdiba aquifer, mean depth 568 ft) overlies Kuwait’s documented strategic freshwater core (1,000 mg/L TDS in the lens center; Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences, 2020; Robinson and Al-Ruwaih, 1985). The 12 wells monitored here are not that core: they sample the lens margins and are predominantly brackish (median 1,116 ppm, range 548 ppm–3,923 ppm), with eight of 12 (%) exceeding 1,000 ppm, so the field-mean of 1,378 ppm should be read as a margin-sample statistic, not as the freshwater-core condition. The Raudhatain lens is reported here for completeness but is held as a strategic reserve, outside the blending optimization (Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences, 2020). In total, the 393-well analytical sample (of which 381 wells form the brackish production network used by the optimization and the remaining 12 are the Raudhatain reserve) spans approximately 40 years of drilling (1952–1990) and four producing-horizon classes (Dual, Kuwait Group, Dammam, and Dibdiba; mixed within fields, Table 3), with field-level mean salinities varying by more than a factor of three (2,694 ppm–4,805 ppm) and aggregate rated production summing to 166.30 MIGD (164.08 MIGD for the brackish network). Turning to the connected storage portion of the system, there are three primary components to consider: ground reservoirs (579 MIG aggregate capacity), elevated tower structures (9.9 MIG), and pumping stations providing a firm total flow rate of 90.7 MIGD together with a separately scheduled standby reserve of 66.6 MIGD. The standby reserve is held to cover station outages, maintenance rotation, and emergency situations rather than routine blending dispatch, and it is, therefore, not counted when determining whether the deliverable pumping bound has been reached: the binding scalar in the optimization is MIGD, the firm aggregate distribution-side throughput reported in the Ministry infrastructure schedule, which is distinct both from the standby reserve and from the well-head rated production of 166.30 MIGD. This figure is the sum of the firm-rated duty throughputs of all pumping stations associated with the brackish-water network as described in the workbook’s infrastructure sheet (firm duty = installed capacity less the largest standby unit per station); it is a single reported aggregate rather than an independently metered flow, and a station-resolved schedule would generally reduce it (Section 6, Limitations). Because the entire binding-constraint conclusion pivots on this single scalar, its value, its dispatchability, and the effect of crediting the 66.6-MIGD standby reserve are stress-tested explicitly in Sections 5, 6. The geographic setting of the five brackish production fields and the Raudhatain reserve, with their rated capacity and mean well-head salinity, is shown in Figure 1.

3.3 Brackish-water quality and blending rationale

Groundwater-quality syntheses for Kuwait report that most groundwater in the Kuwait Group and Dammam Formation is brackish to saline, with TDS generally exceeding potable standards and often falling between 3,000 and 10,000 mg/L (Fanack Water, 2024a; Rashid et al., 2022). Several national studies on the use of water resources note specifically that brackish groundwater with a salinity below approximately 5,000 ppm is already being blended with treated seawater to make drinking water available, and it is also used for irrigation, industrial cooling, and similar non-potable purposes (Mukhopadhyay and Akber, 2018; Al-Ruwaih, 2010). Earlier research has examined optimal blends of desalination-treated water and brackish groundwater from production fields in Kuwait, providing data on the mixes that allow drinking-water standards to be met using a reduced volume of fully desalinated water (Al-Ruwaih, 2010). These findings provide the practical and regulatory basis for treating field-level salinity and TDS thresholds as explicit constraints in the blending-optimization model: the operational TDS limit of 1,000 mg/L at the point of delivery enters as a hard linear constraint, and field-mean salinities (548 ppm–9,460 ppm in the present network) define the per-well coefficients of that constraint. Total dissolved solids is the master variable for both potability and blending suitability in arid-aquifer assessments (Jat Baloch et al., 2021; Saraswat et al., 2023), and the salinity gradients across the Arabian Peninsula’s Gulf aquifers are well-documented (Khan et al., 2022); each well is, therefore, classified by TDS into potable (1,000 ppm), slightly brackish, moderately brackish, and highly brackish bands (Section 5.2) to delimit the feed that can be safely blended. Because reliable major-ion analyses are not available for the full well set, hydrochemical-facies typing (e.g., the Na–Cl and Ca– facies reported for the Salibiya carbonate aquifer; Alhumoud et al., 2010) is taken from the published literature rather than re-derived here, and TDS is used as the operative geochemical constraint.

3.4 Operational and historical datasets

Long-term trends in groundwater usage, abstraction rates, chemical evolution, and aquifer depletion across Kuwait’s primary groundwater production areas are covered in numerous previous studies and national assessments. Historical evaluations in particular (AlAli, 2008; Rashid et al., 2022) describe the development of Kuwait’s primary groundwater fields since the mid-twentieth century, including the growth of well infrastructure, changes in pumping regimes, and long-term trends in the salinity and major-ion concentration of these waters, indicating significant changes in both the quantity and the quality of groundwater under sustained extraction. Recent projects by national research institutions (Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences, 2020) have focused on assessing groundwater-quality changes in key water fields, confirming increases in TDS and documenting spatial heterogeneity in quality within and between fields such as Shagaya, Salibiya, Umm Qudair, and Wafra.

In this study, these published hydrogeological and hydrochemical characterizations are complemented and extended by an internal Arabic brackish-water workbook maintained by the Ministry of Electricity, Water, and Renewable Energy. The workbook collates well-level design specifications, depths, production capacities (IGD), and salinity records for individual wells across Shagaya (sub-fields A-E), Salibiya, Umm Qudair, Wafra, and Atraf for the period 1970–2026, together with associated storage-tank and pumping-station capacities. The national desalination capacities and production trajectories that set the demand context for the blending problem are documented in national water-resource overviews (Fanack Water, 2024b; Mukhopadhyay and Akber, 2018); the cost of desalination versus brackish supply is out of scope here (the LP optimizes physical blendable volume, not cost). The resulting integrated database provides the basis for the linear-programming blending-optimization framework, the polynomial salinity diagnostic, and the sensitivity analysis developed in this study.

4 Materials and methods

4.1 Data preparation

The primary dataset is the Ministry of Electricity, Water, and Renewable Energy’s brackish-groundwater operational record, comprising (i) per-well design data: identifier, drilling date, producing horizons, depth (ft), rated production (IGD), pump capacity (IG ft), well-head salinity (ppm), and structural section; (ii) per-well operational data: status (working/standby/non-operational/abandoned/backfilled), fault category (electrical/mechanical/other), root cause (theft, unconnected, pump lowering, etc.), and responsible repair authority; and (iii) storage and pumping infrastructure: ground-reservoir and elevated-tower capacities, aggregate pumping-station throughput and reserve capacities, and blending delivery zones. The workbook is parsed and harmonized through an automated, reproducible pipeline. The Ministry workbook lists 485 documented brackish wells in total; 393 wells appear in both the design sheet (with depth/salinity/rated-IGD attributes) and the operational sheet (with status/fault attributes) and form the analytical sample. Three nested subsets of this sample are used downstream and are reported here once to avoid ambiguity: all 393 wells underpin the descriptive network statistics (Section 5); the 381 brackish-network wells (the analytical sample minus the 12 Raudhatain reserve) are passed to the optimization (rated capacity 164.08 MIGD); the inferential statistics (ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis, and correlations) use the 379 brackish wells with recorded salinity that fall in fields of ; and the salinity surrogate uses the 374 wells with complete depth, age, and salinity. The remaining 92 entries lack one of the two attribute sets (typically operational status undocumented for early-1950s Salibiya wells or design metadata missing for late-stage Atraf additions) and are excluded from the LP, which requires both salinity and operational status per well. The workbook also under-counts the Wafra field (only two wells in the analytical sample) because it captures wells tied to municipal-blending dispatch; Wafra’s larger agricultural-irrigation well stock is held in separate MEW abstraction-permit records not provided for this study, and the LP, therefore, models only the municipal sub-network at Wafra (see Limitations, Section 6). Across the manuscript, rated production (the sum of well-head design IGD, 166.30 MIGD for the analytical sample) is differentiated from aggregate pumping-station throughput (90.7 MIGD), which is a scalar derived from the Ministry infrastructure schedule and not from the per-well IGD of the wells within a given pumping station. Missing salinity entries are not imputed; the LP simply drops wells lacking salinity (the polynomial surrogate of Section 4.6 is retained only as a diagnostic, not as an imputer, given its modest cross-validated ).

4.2 Network encoding and model resolution

The brackish system is encoded as an attributed well-set with capacity scalars: each well carries design parameters (depth, rated production IGD, and well-head salinity), operational status (working/standby/non-operational/abandoned), and a field tag; storage and pumping infrastructure are summarized as the aggregate capacities reported in Section 3.

Because the distinction governs how every result below should be read, the model’s resolution is stated explicitly, and three levels are separated throughout this study:

  • Well-level asset resolution (resolved here). Each of the 393 wells is an individual decision variable with its own measured salinity, rated capacity, operational status, and fault attribution. This is the level at which the present dataset is genuinely informative and is the study’s empirical contribution.

  • Field- and zone-level aggregation (partially resolved). Wells carry a field tag, and the pumping schedule documents nine stations mapped to five operator delivery zones (Table 5). What the records do not contain is the well-to-station assignment, so the field, station, and zone cannot be joined into a supply topology.

  • Hydraulic distribution-network model (not attempted). No pressure requirement, pipeline head loss, pump curve, reservoir refill rate, or inter-zone transfer restriction is represented. The model contains no hydraulics of any kind.

The present framework is, therefore, properly described as a well-resolved, aggregate-capacity screening model, not a network-resolved optimization, and it is referred to as such throughout. Its purpose is to locate which side of the system binds, not to prescribe station-by-station operation. Two consequences follow and are carried into the principal conclusion rather than confined to the limitations. In the first place, since a capacity matrix for each individual station is generally more restrictive than the aggregate (some wells are hydraulically isolated from the zones requiring their water), the reported optimum is an upper bound on what a station-resolved formulation could deliver. In addition to the capacity issue of stations versus aggregate, there is the assumption of complete hydraulic connection: the LP does not account for hydraulic isolation between wells and zones, so water from any operational well is assumed to reach any zone at no cost. Rather than simply declaring that this assumption has value, its value is quantified in Section 5.8.

4.3 Pumping-station capacity schedule

The aggregate upper bound MIGD imposed on the LP is the total of the firm duty capacities listed in the Ministry infrastructure schedule for each of the individual pumping stations, reproduced in anonymized form in Table 5. Since the entire basis for the conclusion regarding the existence of a binding constraint is predicated upon this single number, its origin is documented completely. (i) The schedule reports, for each station, a daily actual (duty) capacity and a separate reserve capacity; summing these respectively gives the 90.73 MIGD firm figure and the 66.59 MIGD standby figure. (ii) These are design/duty ratings carried in an infrastructure schedule and are not independently metered throughput: the Ministry workbook does contain a sheet for reporting daily well production, against which the ratings could have been checked, but that sheet was supplied empty, so no measured flow record was available to this study and none is claimed. (iii) The schedule is a single undated snapshot of the network as supplied by the Ministry for this study; no operating period, seasonal profile, maintenance derating, or simultaneity factor is annotated in the source, so the LP treats all stations as simultaneously available at their duty rating, which is the most permissive reading and again makes the reported optimum an upper bound. (iv) Two of the nine capacity rows carry no station name in the source and are reported as such. (v) The zone labels are the operator’s own; the asterisk annotation on three of them is carried in the source schedule, and its meaning is not defined in the documentation supplied. Verifying these duty ratings against metered station throughput is the single most valuable piece of additional data collection this study identifies.

4.4 Optimization formulation

Decision variables are the pumping rate (MIGD) for each well and the desalinated-permeate flow (MIGD). The single-objective linear program, with objective Equation 1 and aggregate pumping constraint Equation 4, is (all symbols are collected in Table 6):where ppm (the upper limit of the 100 ppm–1,000 ppm total-dissolved-solids range specified for unbottled drinking water by Gulf Standard GSO 149, which applies in Kuwait through the GCC Standardization Organization (GCC Standardization Organization, 2021; 2009a); see Section 4.5), ppm (typical desalinated permeate), MIGD (reference municipal demand consistent with Fanack Water (2024b)), MIGD (aggregate pumping-station capacity of the brackish network), and encodes well availability under the active scenario. Each MIGD of brackish water successfully blended displaces one MIGD of seawater-desalination throughput. The delivered blended TDS that the TDS constraint controls is the flow-weighted meanand the TDS-limit constraint in the program above is the linear rearrangement of the requirement , with defined by Equation 7, which keeps the optimization a linear program. The pumping-capacity constraint, Equation 4, prevents the LP from prescribing brackish dispatch volumes that exceed the system’s physical distribution-side throughput. Equation 4 is, explicitly, a single aggregate scalar across all pumping stations on the brackish network; a per-station, per-zone constraint matrix would, in general, be more restrictive than the aggregate (some wells may be hydraulically isolated from the zones where their water is demanded), so the LP optimum reported here is an upper bound relative to a station-resolved formulation. A related and additional simplification is that the LP assumes full hydraulic connectivity across the brackish network: water from any operational well is treated as deliverable to any distribution zone at zero additional cost. In the real Kuwait distribution network, the brackish wells in geographically separated fields (Atraf in the west, Wafra in the south, and Salibiya near Kuwait City) likely feed different distribution zones, and the LP’s saturated 90.7 MIGD is, therefore, achievable only in the absence of binding zone-isolation bottlenecks not modeled here. Sensitivity to the aggregate value is examined in Section 5.

4.5 Status of the 1,000 ppm TDS constraint

The 1,000 ppm bound is an operational TDS threshold, and it is important to be precise about what it does and does not certify. The World Health Organization sets no health-based guideline value for total dissolved solids, because no health effect is attributable to TDS as such; TDS is treated as an acceptability parameter governing taste, scaling, and corrosivity, with palatability rated good below 600 mg/L and poor in the 900 mg/L–1,200 mg/L band (World Health Organization, 2003; 2017). Earlier versions of this analysis described the bound as a “WHO potability cap.” That description was incorrect and has been withdrawn throughout.

The applicable regulatory instrument is instead Gulf Standard GSO 149, Unbottled drinking water, which applies in Kuwait through the GCC Standardization Organization, of which Kuwait’s national standards body is a member. The edition currently in force is GSO 149:2021 (Edition 4, approved 1 July 2021), superseding GSO 149:2014 (GCC Standardization Organization, 2021). The edition text openly available to the authors is the notified final draft of the revision superseding GSO 149/2000, whose clause 5.2.3 specifies that “the content of solid substances soluble in unbottled drinking water shall range between 100 and 1,000 ppm” (GCC Standardization Organization, 2009a; GCC Standardization Organization, 2009b); the 1,000-ppm upper limit used here is that value. Two features of that clause matter here. First, it sits under the standard’s quality-related properties heading, alongside color, taste, odor, and pH, and not under the separate table of “chemical components affecting health”—so the standard itself classifies TDS as an acceptability rather than a health parameter (GCC Standardization Organization, 2009a). Second, the range is two-sided: the 100-ppm lower bound means that permeate at ppm is itself non-compliant unless remineralized or blended, which is an independent regulatory motivation for brackish blending beyond volumetric substitution (Nativ et al., 2021; Lu, 2023). The LP imposes only the upper bound, since the delivered blend is above 100 ppm in every scenario reported.

Because the 1,000 ppm figure enters the model as a constraint rather than as commentary, its provenance was audited directly against the issuing body’s own records rather than taken from the secondary literature. Three statements can be made with different degrees of confidence, and they are separated here deliberately. First, the identity of the instrument in force is confirmed from the GSO standards catalog: GSO 149:2021, Unbottled drinking water, Edition 4, a Gulf Technical Regulation approved 1 July 2021 under ICS 13.060.20, superseding GSO 149:2014 (GCC Standardization Organization, 2021).

Second, the wording and—importantly—the placement of the dissolved-solids clause are confirmed from the openly accessible full text of the GSO-notified draft, where clause 5.2.3 sets the 100 ppm–1,000 ppm range under the quality-related properties heading of clause 5.1, while the separate clause 5.2 tabulates “chemical components affecting health” in Tables 1–6 and does not list dissolved solids among them (GCC Standardization Organization, 2009b). This is the documentary basis for treating the bound as an acceptability rather than a health criterion. Third, and stated plainly as a limitation: the consolidated text of the 2021 edition is distributed under license by GSO and its national member bodies and was not available to the authors, so the clause 5.2.3 value has been verified against the accessible edition rather than read off the 2021 document itself. The catalog entry publishes bibliographic metadata only and no clause-level content, so it neither confirms nor contradicts a change to the dissolved-solids range; the authors accordingly do not assert the 2021 wording verbatim, and utilities applying this framework operationally should obtain the licensed edition before using the bound in a dispatch decision.

That residual uncertainty does not propagate to any result reported here, for a reason that is visible in the sensitivity analysis reported in Section 5.7. At the current aggregate pumping capacity of 90.7 MIGD, the pumping constraint—not the TDS constraint—binds at every TDS threshold in the 800 ppm–1,200 ppm sweep, and the optimal blendable volume is 90.70 MIGD across that entire range. The 1,000 ppm bound is, therefore, slack at the operating point: were the applicable threshold to differ anywhere within 20% of the value adopted, every headline quantity in this study—the five-scenario blending volumes, the 1.46 S0S3 uplift, and the finding that the binding constraint sits on the distribution side—would be unchanged. The TDS threshold becomes decision-relevant only above roughly 120 MIGD of pumping capacity, which is the regime the sensitivity sweep was constructed to map.

Consequently, satisfying ppm establishes that a blend is TDS-feasible against the applicable acceptability limit. It does not establish potability: microbial, chemical, radiological, and operational hazards are governed by the risk-based framework of the WHO guidelines and by the microbiological, chemical, and radiological clauses of GSO 149, none of which are evaluated here (World Health Organization, 2017; GCC Standardization Organization, 2021). Every volume reported in this study is accordingly a TDS-feasible blending upper bound, and the words “potable” and “potability” are not used of the model output. Major-ion composition, hardness, sulfate, chloride, boron, and disinfection by-products would each require separate verification before any dispatch schedule derived from this screening model were treated as delivering drinking water.

4.6 Polynomial salinity diagnostic

To test how far well-head salinity can be predicted from observable well attributes (both as a missing-value diagnostic and as a measure of how strongly hydrostratigraphy governs the geochemistry), two data-driven models are benchmarked under one identical, leakage-free protocol (five-fold cross-validation repeated over 10 random seeds, with all preprocessing fit inside each fold; ). Because both models use field as a feature, and wells within a field are spatially and geochemically dependent, a random split leaks field-level information into the test fold. Every model is, therefore, additionally validated under GroupKFold, with field as the grouping variable, so that held-out wells belong to fields absent from training, and under a fully nested cross-validation in which hyperparameters are selected inside each training fold. Both designs are reported in Table 7; the difference between them, not the headline , is the informative quantity. The first is a degree-two polynomial regression on depth and drilling age only; it achieves a modest cross-validated , confirming that single-well covariates alone explain little of the salinity variance, consistent with the hydrogeochemical literature (Rashid et al., 2022; AlAli, 2008; Jat Baloch et al., 2022a), which attributes salinity heterogeneity in the Kuwait Group and Dammam Formation aquifers to producing horizon and structural position rather than depth and age. The second model is a gradient-boosted regression-tree ensemble that adds the producing-horizon and field (structural-section) categoricals; this increases the held-out to 0.529 0.029, a roughly fivefold improvement that directly confirms the mechanism: it is hydrostratigraphic information (horizon, field), not the two single-well covariates, that carries the predictive signal for well-head salinity. This is itself a result for data-driven water management: salinity prediction in this multi-aquifer system becomes tractable only once hydrostratigraphic features are supplied. Even so, an of remains below the accuracy a surrogate would need to feed the hard 1,000-ppm TDS constraint safely: the gradient-boosted model’s cross-validated RMSE is 855 ppm (computed on the public decade-rounded dataset), an out-of-sample error comparable in magnitude to the 1,000-ppm limit itself. Measured well-head salinity is, therefore, used directly in the optimization, and the learned models are retained as a salinity diagnostic rather than as an imputer.

4.7 Scenarios

Five intervention scenarios are evaluated:

  • S0: Baseline: current operational status only (working and standby wells).

  • S1: Mechanical rehabilitation: restore all non-operational wells carrying a mechanical fault tag (pump replacement or reconnection); wells additionally carrying an electrical fault are not excluded, so the scenarios overlap, which does not affect the saturated result.

  • S2: Electrical rehabilitation including security: restore all wells with electrical failures, including those affected by cable/switchgear theft.

  • S3: Combined (S1S2): both mechanical and electrical rehabilitation.

  • S4: Full restoration plus new drilling: S3 with a uniform 10% uplift applied to every well’s rated capacity, a sensitivity proxy for new drilling rather than the addition of discrete marginal wells (sensitivity analysis only). Boundary-condition stress tests on demand (climate-driven cooling and water requirements) enter at this stage as scenario assumptions, not as the central object of study.

4.8 Statistical analysis of the well-field geochemistry

Before optimization, the hydrogeochemical structure of the well network is characterized with inferential statistics, following the data-driven groundwater-quality assessment practice now standard in the field (Jat Baloch et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Lv et al., 2022). Well-head salinity is strongly heteroscedastic across the production fields: the largest field variance exceeds the smallest by a factor of 78, and both Levene’s test (, ) and its Brown–Forsythe median-centered form (, ) reject equal variances decisively. The classical one-way test and Tukey’s HSD both assume homoscedasticity and are, therefore, not appropriate as primary tests here; earlier versions of this analysis reported them, and they have been replaced. The primary test of the between-field salinity difference is now Welch’s heteroscedasticity-robust ANOVA, cross-checked against the Brown–Forsythe statistic and the non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test, and the post hoc procedure is the Games–Howell test, which uses Welch-corrected degrees of freedom per pair and is valid under unequal variances and unequal group sizes. Effect size is reported as , as the less upward-biased , and as the one-way random-effects intra-class correlation, which is the interpretable quantity for the between- versus within-field question: it estimates the share of total salinity variance attributable to field identity. The classical is retained in the text only as a reference point against the previous version. Bivariate associations between salinity and the available well covariates (depth, age, and rated yield) are quantified with both the Pearson product-moment coefficient (Equation 8) and the Spearman rank coefficient , computed both pooled across all wells and within the largest single-field sub-networks (to separate between-field from within-aquifer structure and guard against Simpson’s paradox):with defined identically on rank-transformed variables to capture monotonic but non-linear structure. Wells are additionally binned by total dissolved solids into hydrochemical classes (potable 1,000 ppm, slightly brackish 1,000 ppm–3,000 ppm, moderately brackish 3,000 ppm–5,000 ppm, and highly brackish 5,000 ppm–10,000 ppm) to summarize the blendable feed band. Significance is assessed at . The Raudhatain freshwater lens is excluded from these tests as it is a strategic reserve outside the brackish blending network. All statistics are computed in an open, reproducible routine on the brackish network (the 393-well analytical sample excluding the 12 Raudhatain wells), restricted to the 379 wells with recorded salinity in fields of for the field-comparison tests.

5 Results

5.1 Network description

The full analytical sample comprises 393 design-recorded wells (Table 4); excluding the 12-well Raudhatain freshwater lens (reserved as a strategic resource and not blended) the brackish production network used by the optimization comprises 381 wells with a combined rated capacity of 164.08 MIGD. Of the 393 wells, 86 are currently working and 36 are on standby; 224 (57.0%) are non-operational, and the remainder are backfilled, abandoned, transferred, or of unrecorded operational status (Figure 2a). Among all assessed wells carrying a recorded fault, 165 have an electrical fault (the majority documented as cable/switchgear theft) and 80 a mechanical fault; because some wells carry a fault while on standby or in transfer, these fault counts span a larger pool than the strictly non-operational set. Salinity in the assessed wells ranges from 548 to 9,460 ppm (mean 4,033 ppm); the field-level mean salinity peaks at Wafra (5,000 ppm, but only two wells in the municipal sample) and, among the larger fields, at Salibiya (4,805 ppm); within the Shagaya sub-fields, it is the highest at Shagaya E (4,136 ppm) and the lowest at Shagaya D (2,694 ppm) (Figure 2b; per-field breakdown in Figure 3). Figure 4 integrates these three dimensions (geochemistry, deliverable capacity, and asset condition) at field resolution: the largest-capacity field (Umm Qudair) also carries the highest operational fraction, whereas the Salibiya field combines high salinity, large size, and a low operational fraction, marking it as the principal rehabilitation target.

5.2 Hydrogeochemical structure of the well network

Well-head salinity differs significantly among the production fields (across the eight field/sub-field units with sufficient sample, the five Shagaya sub-fields together with Salibiya, Umm Qudair, and Atraf, the two-well Wafra field being excluded by the criterion). Because the field variances differ by a factor of 78 (Levene , ; Brown–Forsythe , ), the heteroscedasticity-robust Welch test is used as the primary test: , . Two independent cross-checks agree, the Brown–Forsythe and the non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis , and the Games–Howell post hoc, which is valid under unequal variances, separates 21 of the 28 field pairs. Correcting the test choice strengthens rather than weakens the conclusion: the robust Welch statistic is substantially larger than the classical of reported previously, because the homoscedastic pooled-variance denominator was diluted by a few high-variance fields. The corresponding Tukey HSD post hoc had identified 15 of the 28 pairs; Games–Howell identifies 21, so the earlier procedure was also conservative here. The fields, therefore, differ significantly in mean well-head salinity. The between-field effect is large by every estimator: , , and a one-way random-effects intra-class correlation of 0.41; i.e., field identity alone accounts for roughly 41% of the total well-head salinity variance, leaving the remainder within the fields. Producing-horizon membership is, however, mixed within fields (Table 3): a complementary Welch ANOVA grouped by normalized horizon (Dammam, dual, and Kuwait Group) is itself significant (, ) but explains far less of the salinity variance than the by-field grouping . The between- and within-field components can be separated directly: once each well’s salinity is centered on its own field mean, the horizon effect vanishes entirely (, , ). Producing horizon, therefore, carries essentially no within-field information about salinity in this network; its apparent effect is a by-product of which horizons each field taps. This is the clearest statement the data support of the between- versus within-field separation, and it is why the optimization is encoded at field-and-well resolution rather than by horizon. The strong between-field salinity contrast is thus a field-scale signal (reflecting structural position, abstraction history, and mixed horizon membership together) rather than a clean hydrostratigraphic partition, and it justifies the field-resolved encoding used by the optimization rather than a single network-mean salinity. Pooled across all fields, salinity is negatively correlated with depth (Pearson , Spearman , ); caution is warranted, however, because this pooled gradient is largely a between-field effect, a Simpson’s-paradox risk when non-exchangeable aquifer units are combined. Within the three largest single-field sub-networks, the depth–salinity correlation is significant only at Salibiya (, ) and is effectively absent at Umm Qudair (, ) and Atraf (, ). Depth is, therefore, a between-field proxy for which aquifer a well taps rather than a universal within-aquifer driver, consistent with salinity being governed primarily by producing horizon and structural position (Rashid et al., 2022; Alhumoud et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2024; Jat Baloch et al., 2022a). Salinity shows only a weak positive association with well age (, on exact drilling dates; , , i.e., non-significant, when recomputed on the decade-rounded public dataset) (too weak, and too confounded by horizon membership and abstraction history, to support a causal abstraction-driven-salinization interpretation) and a weak negative association with the rated yield (, ); both are reported as descriptive associations only. The full inter-attribute correlation structure is shown in Figure 5. By hydrochemical class, 99.7% of wells exceed the 1,000-ppm TDS threshold (confirming the field is brackish by definition), and 81.1% fall in the 1,000 ppm–5,000 ppm band that is most suitable as a blending feed; the per-class counts and field means provide the per-well coefficients of the optimization’s TDS constraint.

FIGURE 5

5.3 Salinity surrogate performance

A controlled head-to-head benchmark of the two salinity models (Table 7; one identical leakage-free five-fold cross-validation repeated over 10 seeds, ) quantifies how much hydrostratigraphic information the prediction requires. The depth-and-age polynomial reaches only , whereas the gradient-boosted ensemble that additionally encodes producing-horizon and field (structural-section) categoricals reaches , a near-fivefold gain. Well-head salinity is, therefore, predictable in this multi-aquifer system, but only when the hydrostratigraphic structure is supplied; depth and age alone are weak predictors. Because even the stronger model’s accuracy remains insufficient to feed the hard 1,000-ppm constraint safely; measured well-head salinity is used directly in the optimization, and both models are retained as a geochemical diagnostic (Section 4.6).

The validation design deserves emphasis, because the random-split figure above is optimistic in a way that is easy to miss. Random -fold cross-validation places wells from the same field in both the training and the test fold, so the model can succeed by learning each field’s mean salinity and assigning held-out wells to it. Re-running the identical models under GroupKFold on field, so that every held-out well belongs to a field entirely absent from training, collapses performance below the intercept-only baseline: for the gradient-boosted model (RMSE 1,368 ppm) and for the polynomial (RMSE 1,602 ppm). The same conclusion follows from the complementary direction: when predictions and observations are both centered on their field mean, the gradient-boosted model explains only of the remaining within-field variation. Tuning is not the issue, as a fully nested cross-validation with hyperparameters selected inside each training fold returns , which is statistically indistinguishable from the fixed-hyperparameter random-CV result.

The honest reading is, therefore, that the models have learned which field a well belongs to, not how salinity varies within an aquifer. This is consistent with the variance decomposition above (field identity carries 41% of total salinity variance, and horizon carries none once field is removed), and it sharpens rather than softens the study’s existing methodological conclusion: a surrogate that cannot extrapolate to an unseen field, and that explains almost none of the within-field variation, must not be placed inside a hard-constrained dispatch optimization. Measured salinity is used throughout, and the surrogate’s role is confined to quantifying how strongly hydrostratigraphy governs the geochemistry.

5.4 Five-scenario blending results

Table 8 reports the linear-programming solution for each of the five intervention scenarios; Figure 6 visualizes the resulting brackish-blendable volume and the corresponding delivered TDS. Under current operations (S0), the network supports 62.24 MIGD of brackish blending (11.97% of municipal supply, delivered TDS 516 ppm). The baseline is itself instructive: at S0, the system is well-availability-bound: the 62.24 MIGD dispatched equals the summed rated capacity of the eligible working-plus-standby wells, with both the pumping and TDS limits slack. Mechanical rehabilitation alone (S1) increases the blendable volume to 90.70 MIGD, at which point the aggregate pumping-station-capacity constraint (Equation 4, MIGD) becomes active. The most informative structural feature of the result is, therefore, this regime switch: S0S1 moves the network from a well-availability regime into a pumping-bound regime, and it is the transition (not a continued well-availability story) that the 1.46 uplift records. Because pumping capacity binds in S1, the subsequent scenarios, electrical-fault rehabilitation (S2: 90.70 MIGD), full combined rehabilitation (S3: 90.70 MIGD), and the 10% new-drilling sensitivity (S4: 90.70 MIGD), all return the same maximum blendable volume of 90.7 MIGD. Across these saturated scenarios, the LP redistributes flow over a progressively larger eligible well pool, modestly improving blended TDS (S1 723 ppm, S2 768 ppm, S3 731 ppm, and S4 729 ppm) but extracting no additional blendable volume. The overall S0S3 uplift is 1.46 (62.24 90.70 MIGD), with the upper bound set by the distribution-side pumping network, not by the brackish well pool.

5.5 Greedy baseline and lexicographic LP

To benchmark the LP, it is compared against a transparent sorted-by-salinity greedy heuristic: working and standby wells are dispatched in the ascending order of well-head salinity until either the pumping cap or the blended-TDS feasibility limit is reached (analogous to the operational rule of “blend the freshest wells first” noted in Mukhopadhyay and Akber (2018); Al-Ruwaih (2010)). On the saturated scenarios, the greedy and LP achieve the same blendable volume of 90.70 MIGD; on the baseline (S0), they tie at 62.24 MIGD. The LP’s value over the greedy is, therefore, not in total throughput but in flexibility: the LP can place dispatch on any subset of wells whose blended TDS satisfies the limit, whereas the greedy is locked to the lowest-salinity feasible portfolio. This is a useful diagnostic: it shows that the single-objective LP solution is non-unique under the present constraints: multiple portfolios saturate pumping at the TDS-feasible blend.

To resolve the non-uniqueness substantively rather than merely diagnose it, a lexicographic two-stage LP is reported. Stage 1 solves the primary problem and records the saturated volume MIGD. Stage 2 re-solves with a secondary objective subject to (with MIGD, the LP-solver feasibility tolerance; this is six orders of magnitude smaller than the saturated volume and is, therefore, numerically equivalent to a strict equality at machine precision), picking the unique lowest-TDS dispatch portfolio that still saturates pumping. Under S3, the lexicographic LP returns 90.70 MIGD at a blended TDS of 613 ppm, dispatching 187 wells, which is a TDS improvement of 118 ppm relative to the primary LP’s portfolio (731 ppm and 221 wells) at no measurable volume cost. The lexicographic portfolio coincides with the sorted-by-salinity greedy baseline (which is expected, since dispatching wells in ascending well-head salinity is by construction lex-optimal for the min-TDS secondary objective) confirming that the LP’s flexibility advantage over the greedy lies elsewhere (e.g., the ability to support alternative secondary objectives such as minimizing pumped distance, prioritizing security-protected wells, or balancing across fields). For deployment, the lexicographic LP is recommended as the default formulation: it delivers a unique, reproducible dispatch portfolio with a lower delivered TDS at no cost to volume.

5.6 Sensitivity to municipal demand

To stress-test the headline result against demand variability, the S3 LP is re-solved across a 15% envelope of municipal demand: MIGD in 20 MIGD steps. Across this range, the brackish-blendable volume remains saturated at 90.70MIGD (pumping is always binding under S3 at any demand in the sampled grid), confirming the robustness of the binding-constraint finding to seasonal and inter-annual demand variation. The brackish blend share of total supply, however, varies monotonically with : from 20.61% at MIGD (lower demand, fewer SWRO/MSF units required, and higher blend share) to 15.12% at MIGD (peak demand, blend share diluted by the larger desalinated component). The central case of MIGD yields 17.44%, consistent with current Kuwait operations (Fanack Water, 2024b; Tariq et al., 2022). Figure 7 shows both responses: the brackish blend share decreases monotonically with demand while the delivered blended TDS adjusts as the optimizer re-weights the dispatched well portfolio, and in every case, the brackish volume stays pinned at the pumping-saturated ceiling. The delivered TDS falls over most of the envelope (854.9 ppm at to 660.6 ppm at ) but turns up slightly at the highest demand (684.7 ppm at ): once the permeate requirement is large enough, the saturated 90.70 MIGD must be met from a marginally different TDS-feasible well subset, which is a boundary re-weighting effect at the envelope edge rather than a reversal of the underlying monotone share trend.

5.7 Sensitivity to the pumping-capacity and TDS constraints

To map how the binding constraint shifts across plausible upgrades, the pumping bound is swept over MIGD against the TDS bound ppm under the S3 (combined-rehabilitation) well pool. Figure 8 shows the resulting blendable volume and the constraint that is binding in each cell. Three regimes emerge: (i) at the current pumping cap of 90.7 MIGD and at 100 MIGD, the pumping constraint binds for every TDS level (blendable volume saturates at the pumping bound; the TDS limit is slack); (ii) at 120 MIGD–140 MIGD pumping, the regime is mixed: pumping binds at higher TDS limits, and TDS binds at lower TDS limits, with the transition crossing the diagonal of Figure 8; (iii) at 160 MIGD–200 MIGD pumping, the TDS limit is the binding constraint across all TDS levels in the sampled grid (blendable volume is independent of further pumping expansion). At the 1,000 ppm TDS threshold with unconstrained pumping, the maximum feasible blend is 135.63 MIGD; closing the gap from the current 90.70 MIGD to this upper bound requires both pumping-side investment (to push beyond the saturation point) and dispatch-side optimization (to reach the TDS-feasible frontier). The combined design implication is that pumping expansion alone yields diminishing returns past 140 MIGD–160 MIGD; beyond that, additional volume requires either lower-TDS wells (e.g., the Raudhatain freshwater reserve, which are currently held back) or relaxation of the TDS threshold (e.g., via reverse-osmosis polishing).
