5.8 What the aggregate-capacity assumption is worth

The single most consequential simplification in this model is that the 90.73 MIGD of firm pumping capacity is treated as one pooled scalar, so that any well can serve any zone (Section 4.2). The station schedule (Table 5) shows that this pool is, in fact, divided across nine stations and five delivery zones, the largest zone holding 35.19 MIGD and the smallest 7.60 MIGD, with no single station exceeding 23% of the total. Because the well-to-station assignment is not documented, the effect of that division is bounded here by ensemble rather than asserted by assumption: the LP is re-solved with one capacity constraint per station instead of one pooled constraint, over 2,000 admissible assignments of wells to stations, and the resulting distribution of realizable volume is compared against the aggregate optimum of 90.73 MIGD.

Two assignment regimes bracket the answer. When wells are allocated individually to stations in proportion to each station’s firm capacity (that is, the probability of assigning a well to a station equals that station’s share of total firm capacity), the aggregate upper limit is found to be very close to the actual maximum attainable: median 90.73 MIGD, fifth percentile 89.58 MIGD. In this regime, no capacity is stranded because every station receives a well pool much larger than its own duty rating; the S3-eligible rated well capacity, 146.09 MIGD, exceeds firm pumping capacity by roughly 60%. In contrast, when the well pool of an entire producing field is forced to feed a single station—a constraint grounded in physical reality, given that the fields are geographically separate and trunk-main connected—the realizable volume falls to a median of only 55.08 MIGD (fifth–95th percentile 39.41 MIGD–68.82 MIGD), which is 61% of the aggregate optimum. Put the other way, the aggregate formulation over-estimates deliverable volume by approximately 39% once supply cannot be freely rerouted between zones because capacity stranded in a zone whose local fields cannot fill it is capacity that does not exist. This is the quantitative content of the upper-bound qualification, and it is carried into the conclusion.

Two points survive this correction, and they are the ones on which the study rests. First, although the numbers change with each draw, the direction of the finding is constant across all draws: distribution-side capacity, not well availability, limits the volume that can be delivered in 100% of the 2,000 station-resolved solutions, precisely because even the pessimistic field-clustered median of 55.08 MIGD lies far below the 146.09 MIGD of eligible-rated well capacity. Restricting connectivity, therefore, makes the distribution side bind harder, never less. Second, restricting connectivity sharpens the policy implications of this study rather than reversing them: if the realistic figure is closer to 55.08 MIGD than to 90.73 MIGD, then pumping capacity is maldistributed among zones to a degree that is itself a first-order lever, and the return to re-balancing or interconnecting existing capacity may rival the return to installing more of it. Neither quantity can be evaluated without the well-to-station connectivity record, which is accordingly the primary data request this study makes of the operator.

6 Discussion

6.1 Pumping capacity, not well availability, is the binding constraint

The principal finding of this study is that Kuwait’s aggregate distribution-side pumping-station capacity constrains the operationally achievable blendable volume under the LP formulation—not the upstream brackish well pool. Mechanical rehabilitation alone (S1) saturates the aggregate pumping capacity of 90.7 MIGD; subsequent upstream interventions (S2 electrical, S3 combined, and S4 plus new drilling) return the same blendable volume but draw on a progressively broader and lower-mean-salinity well pool, which the LP exploits to improve delivered TDS without increasing throughput. This claim is valid at the system level only, being derived from a single-scalar pumping abstraction (Section 4.2); in the real distribution network, pumping is per-station and per-zone. The station schedule is now reported in full (Table 5), and the cost of the aggregation is quantified in Section 5.8: the 90.73 MIGD figure is an upper bound, and a station-resolved network in which each field feeds one station realizes a median of only 55.08 MIGD. What remains unavailable, and what would be needed to replace the bound with a determinate value, is the well-to-station connectivity record. The aggregate pumping bound is identified as binding; which station-level physical bottleneck (motor capacity, hydraulic head loss, valve sizing, or upstream-tank refill rate) constitutes the proximate constraint at any specific station is not resolved here. The policy implication is, therefore, co-investigation of distribution-side capacity, with pumping the leading hypothesis, rather than a pre-committed investment in pumping motors alone. The implication for planning is nonetheless robust at the system level: brackish-well rehabilitation alone cannot push blendable volume above the network’s aggregate pumping throughput, and the marginal return of further upstream investment past the S1 saturation point is realized through TDS improvement and well-pool diversification, not through additional volume.

Two features make this finding robust rather than an artefact of the optimization. First, the headline does not rest on the optimization machinery alone: the firm pumping throughput (90.7 MIGD) is well below the rehabilitated pool’s rated production (166.30 MIGD), so any reasonable dispatch rule (the LP or the sort-by-salinity greedy heuristic, which ties the LP on volume across all saturated scenarios) saturates the pumping bound. The LP’s distinct contribution is, therefore, not the saturated volume (the capacity comparison already implies it) but the dispatch portfolio: it guarantees TDS feasibility, and its lexicographic stage minimizes delivered TDS to yield a unique, reproducible well schedule (Section 5), the value a one-line greedy rule cannot provide once secondary objectives or feasibility guarantees matter. Second, the finding survives two explicit stress tests, both recomputed on the public dataset. (a) Spatial disaggregation. Partitioning the brackish fields into three coarse geographic distribution zones (north/Atraf, 27.4 MIGD eligible; central/Salibiya–Shagaya, 74.2 MIGD; and southwest/Umm Qudair–Wafra, 44.5 MIGD) and splitting the 90.7-MIGD firm capacity across them degrades the realizable blended volume only marginally (to 87.8 MIGD under an equal three-way split and 89.9 MIGD under a demand-weighted split, versus 90.7 MIGD when the split tracks each zone’s rated capacity) because every zone’s eligible rated capacity comfortably exceeds its pump share. That test used a hypothetical three-way geographic partition and hypothetical pump shares, and the reassuring conclusion does not survive the station-level schedule now available (Table 5). The stronger analysis of Section 5.8, which uses the documented per-station capacities, shows the shortfall is small only when wells can be assigned to stations individually; under the realistic constraint that a whole field feeds one station, it reaches 39%. The previous “at most 3%” statement is, therefore, withdrawn, and the aggregate optimum is treated throughout as an upper bound whose realistic value may be nearer to 55.08 MIGD. What the disaggregation does not do is change the direction of the finding, since the distribution side binds in 100% of station-resolved solutions. (b) Reserve crediting. Crediting the full 66.6 MIGD standby reserve (combined 157.3 MIGD) increases the optimum to 135.63 MIGD, but the binding constraint then shifts to the 1,000 ppm operational TDS threshold (delivered TDS 1,000 ppm), not to well availability: the 146.1 MIGD of eligible-rated well capacity remains slack even then. The robust, basis-independent statement is, therefore, stronger than “pumping binds”: well rehabilitation is never the binding lever. A downstream constraint (distribution-side pumping at firm capacity or the TDS threshold once the reserve is credited) limits blendable volume first across the entire realistic capacity range, so the qualitative conclusion does not hinge on the precise value of 90.7 MIGD. The sweep (Figure 8) is consistent, holding the regime pump-bound at every TDS level up to 140 MIGD and TDS-bound above.

The LP-implied 1:1 displacement of seawater desalination per MIGD of brackish blending is a direct consequence of the demand equality with fixed at 520 MIGD: every additional unit of brackish dispatch mechanically reduces the desalinated-permeate flow by the same amount. The realized displacement in operation is bounded below this theoretical 1:1 figure: Kuwait’s MSF and SWRO plants are cogeneration-coupled to thermal-power blocks, so in summer, the desalination plants cannot dial back without curtailing electricity, and in winter, the inverse holds (Ghaffour et al., 2013). A key aspect of these results is that the S3 ceiling of 90.70 MIGD represents an upper limit on blending-side substitution under current pumping assets and does not represent an expected outcome of actual dispatch.

In the context of Kuwait’s high per capita demand (165 ) and 92%-desalination dependence (Fanack Water, 2024b; Tariq et al., 2022), this maximum volume offers some degree of improved supply diversity; the planning implication, however, is that if Kuwait wishes to improve its water supply beyond what is possible with the existing pumping network, rehabilitation of the brackish groundwater resource will have to be coordinated with upgrading that network.

6.2 Theft and the political economy of asset loss

Several characteristics of the dataset relate to electrical faults, and the most important is that most wells in the electrical-fault group have their primary reason for being unable to function attributed to theft, typically of copper cabling and switchgear: 165 wells are unavailable for this reason, which is the single largest documented failure category. These losses occur mainly in remote desert locations around Shagaya, Atraf, and Salibiya, where wells are spread over long distances, perimeter surveillance is poor, and copper has a ready resale market. The same pattern occurs among other utilities across the Gulf region and North Africa operating in similarly sparsely populated desert terrain. Inter-agency coordination required to prevent such theft involves three bodies: the Ministry of Electricity, Water, and Renewable Energy owns the assets, the Ministry of Interior is tasked with criminal investigation, and the Kuwait Municipality controls the land-use permissions needed for perimeter works; coordination among the three is a recognized bottleneck. An effective rehabilitation program must, therefore, include a security and asset-protection component (perimeter surveillance, cable burial, GPS-tagged copper, and rapid-replacement contracts for damaged equipment) rather than treating the wells as a purely technical refurbishment problem. Although the LP shows no incremental benefit from theft remediation in terms of additional volume, since pumping binds first, its marginal return appears instead as improved delivered TDS and a more diversified well pool; and the cumulative cost of repeated theft-driven outages remains a significant component of MEW operating expenditure that falls outside the LP framing of the present study. The binding-constraint finding also has a governance corollary: because the lever is distribution-side, the primary investment decision sits with whoever owns pumping and transmission capital rather than with the well-rehabilitation directorate, so capturing the uplift requires a single budget line that co-stages well-rehabilitation and pumping-capacity upgrades and an institutional owner for that joint decision, which is a coordination problem of the same shape as, and partly overlapping, the three-ministry theft-prevention gap above.

6.3 The polynomial salinity diagnostic, and why it stays a diagnostic

The depth-and-age polynomial explains only a small fraction of well-head salinity variance ( over 10 seeds; Section 5), an out-of-sample error of the same order as the 1,000-ppm TDS threshold. Imputation of missing salinities with such a surrogate would, therefore, inject TDS-constraint noise comparable in magnitude to the constraint itself, which is operationally unsafe. The gradient-boosted model that additionally encodes producing-horizon and field structure reaches , a roughly five-fold improvement, yet its cross-validated RMSE of 855 ppm still falls short of the accuracy required to feed the hard 1,000-ppm limit. From a methodological perspective, there are two lessons: (i) the salinity variability observed across the Kuwait Group and Dammam Formation aquifer systems is governed primarily by the producing horizon, structural position, and sub-field-scale flow paths rather than by the single-well covariates of depth and age, consistent with the hydrogeochemical record (Rashid et al., 2022; AlAli, 2008); and (ii) a surrogate capable of earning a place within the LP would require hydrostratigraphic features and a substantially higher held-out . The practical implication for operational decision-making is that decisions should rest upon measured rather than predicted well-head TDS, and that investment in real-time TDS measurement equipment at the operational subset of wells—such instrumentation being currently undocumented in the Ministry workbook—would yield a high marginal return.

6.4 Energy and carbon implications of the implied displacement

The energy and carbon figures in this subsection are order-of-magnitude scoping estimates, not outputs of the optimization; a dedicated life-cycle assessment is out of scope and a deliberate next step. With that caveat, the implied displacement maps to an approximate footprint via standard desalination intensities. The blending-side substitution increases from 62.24 MIGD already displaced at baseline (S0) to 90.70 MIGD at S3, an incremental 28.46 MIGD attributable to the rehabilitation program. Taking the regional ranges of 10 kWh–16 kWh for MSF and 3 kWh–4 kWh for SWRO, electrical-equivalent (Ghaffour et al., 2013),1 a 60/40 MSF/SWRO mix gives a blended intensity of kWh . One MIGD (4,546 ) sustained for a year, therefore, corresponds to 12 GWh–19 GWh and, at a 0.65 e grid factor (gas-and-oil-dominated Kuwait grid), 8–12 e. Applied to the 28.46 MIGD rehabilitation increment, this is (as an upper-bound theoretical avoidance contingent on cogeneration dispatch flexibility) on the order of 340 GWh–530 GWh of avoided desalination energy and 220–345 e of avoided emissions; scaled to the full 90.70 MIGD displaced at S3, the figures are larger. The realized avoidance is bounded below these upper bounds by the cogeneration coupling discussed in Section 6 (§5.1): when MSF plants run to satisfy electricity load, dialing back their throughput is constrained, so a fraction of the brackish blending may not translate into MSF reduction in the same season.

6.5 SDG 6 alignment and policy implications

The framework supports SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), specifically target 6.4 (water-use efficiency and sustainable withdrawals) and target 6.5 (integrated water resources management) (UNESCO, 2019; Eawag, 2024). Rehabilitation increases the dispatched brackish volume by the relative gain given in Equation 9where denotes brackish blendable volume (MIGD). This 45.7% (62.24 90.70 MIGD) is an increase in the volume of brackish water substituted for desalination (that is, in desalination-substitution capacity) and is expressly not the UN indicator-6.4.1 water-use-efficiency ratio (value added per of water used, US$ ), which this study does not compute. It is best read as a contribution to the sustainable-withdrawal intent of target 6.4 and to IWRM (target 6.5), not as an indicator-6.4.1 efficiency figure. Two sustainability qualifications attach to it. First, increasing abstraction from a largely non-renewable brackish resource (Al-Zubari, 2003) bears directly on indicator 6.4.2 (water stress, withdrawal relative to available resource), which would move adversely and is not quantified here. Second, the LP optimizes a short-run operational ceiling with no multi-year safe-yield constraint; whether sustained 90.70 MIGD abstraction lies within the fields’ renewable or prudent-depletion yield is out of scope but essential before implementation, and would enter the LP as an additional per-field annual-abstraction bound linked to Al-Eisa (2020). Four policy implications follow. (i) Brackish-well rehabilitation must be co-scoped with pumping-network capacity expansion; isolated well-rehabilitation programs will deliver no additional blendable volume beyond the S1 saturation point. (ii) Sequencing matters: because pumping binds before electrical rehabilitation makes a difference at the aggregate level, the marginal return of theft-remediation investment is realized through TDS improvement and lower-mean-salinity dispatching, not through additional volume. (iii) Security measures (cable burial and perimeter monitoring) should be treated as a co-investment with technical rehabilitation. (iv) The pipeline used here is well within current operational capability, requiring only the operational and design records already maintained by the utility plus modest computing resources. What is transferred to other utilities that are also in arid states is the diagnostic method and not the Kuwait-specific numbers: any such utility should compare its firm distribution-side throughput with its rehabilitated rated well capacity before sequencing investment in well rehabilitation. The only data necessary to begin the analysis are firm-versus-reserve pumping by zone, per-well salinity and status, and demand. That distribution-side capacity binds before well availability is an empirical observation for Kuwait, based upon its particular topology of pumping and demand, and must, therefore, be re-derived elsewhere.

6.6 Discrepancies, counter-readings, and what the result does not mean

There are four areas of tension in these results that are stated plainly rather than smoothed over.

The headline volume is not a forecast, and more blending is not the same as more water. The LP determines the maximum amount of brackish water to dispatch subject to fixed demand equality, so each additional MIGD of brackish water displaces a MIGD of permeate. It, therefore, does not produce additional supply, and it should not be interpreted as an incentive to produce more desalinated water; the correct interpretation is that a lower-energy source replaces a higher-energy one within a fixed delivery obligation. Whether that replacement is realized depends on cogeneration dispatch, which this model does not represent.

The aggregate and station-resolved results disagree by almost a factor of two, and the disagreement is informative.Section 5.8 presents 90.73 MIGD under full connectivity and 55.08 MIGD under field-clustered connectivity. Instead of reporting only the favorable figure, both are carried forward: the first represents what the network could accomplish if capacity were perfectly shareable, whereas the second approximates what it can accomplish as constructed. The difference between them measures how much value is embedded in the topology of the network, and it is arguably a more actionable planning quantity than either endpoint.

The salinity model succeeds and fails simultaneously. A gradient-boosted model achieving under random cross-validation would ordinarily be reported as a useful predictor. Under field-held-out validation, however, it performs worse than predicting the global mean. Both facts are reported because both are true of different tasks: the model interpolates within known fields but cannot extrapolate to new ones. A reader who took only the first number into account would draw the wrong operational conclusion, which is precisely why the surrogate is excluded from the optimization.

Meeting a TDS threshold is a weak claim, intentionally. The 1,000-ppm constraint is an acceptability limit and not a health-based limit, and clearing it establishes only TDS feasibility (Section 4.5). A blend can satisfy that limit while still failing on sulfate, chloride, hardness, boron, or microbiological criteria, none of which are evaluated in this study. The model identifies where a volumetric ceiling lies; it does not certify water.

6.7 Limitations

Twelve limitations should be noted. First, the well-head salinity record is single-time-stamp rather than time-series, so long-term aquifer-drawdown effects are not explicitly modeled, a known feature of the Kuwait Group and Dammam aquifers (Rashid et al., 2022; Al-Eisa, 2020). Second, the optimization assumes static aquifer response and a single demand scenario; coupling to daily peak-demand variation (the subject of a companion study) is left to future work. Third, the energy and carbon translation in Section 6 rests on plant-fleet-average intensities from Ghaffour et al. (2013); year-on-year fuel-mix variation and cogeneration coupling will modulate the exact magnitude of realized displacement. Fourth, the aggregate pumping-station capacity ( MIGD) and the municipal demand ( MIGD) enter the LP as fixed scalars; spatial heterogeneity of pumping load, per-station capacity allocation, and seasonal demand are not resolved here. The binding role of pumping capacity should, therefore, be interpreted as a system-level finding rather than a station-by-station prescription. The per-station duty and standby ratings underlying the aggregate are now reported (Table 5), and the effect of the aggregation is bounded in Section 5.8; what remains missing is the well-to-station assignment, without which a genuinely station-resolved LP cannot be built. Fifth, the Ministry workbook contains only two recorded wells in the Wafra field even though Wafra is operationally a principal agricultural abstraction zone. The workbook under-represents Wafra because it captures only the wells tied to municipal-blending dispatch; the agricultural-irrigation wells in Wafra are recorded in separate MEW abstraction-permit records not provided to this study. The per-field results for Wafra should, therefore, be read as municipal-only and not as a comprehensive Wafra-field assessment. Sixth, the Atraf field (81 wells, KW horizon) has the thinnest peer-reviewed hydrogeochemical context in the available literature: Al-Eisa (2020) addressed the Eocene (Dammam) aquifer at central Kuwait rather than the KW horizon at Atraf, and no Atraf-specific peer-reviewed hydrochemical time series equivalent to Alhumoud et al. (2010) for Salibiya was located. The Atraf salinity coefficients in the LP, therefore, rely most heavily on Ministry workbook values rather than independent published verification, although the field-mean Atraf salinity (4,593 ppm) sits within the multi-field range reported by Rashid et al. (2022). Seventh, the binding role of the pumping-capacity constraint was verified independently of the modeling narrative: every reported number is regenerated deterministically from the source operational records by the open analysis pipeline (fixed random seeds; Section 5.2), so the headline can be re-derived end-to-end from the raw data rather than taken on the authors’ word. Eighth, the raw Ministry workbook is restricted under MEW data-sharing policy; the anonymized per-well derived dataset and full analysis code accompanying this study (Data Availability Statement) nonetheless reproduce every reported figure, table, and statistic without access to the restricted source, so reproducibility does not depend on Ministry liaison. Ninth, the LP assumes full hydraulic connectivity across the brackish network: any operational well is treated as deliverable to any distribution zone at no additional cost. In practice, the Atraf (western), Wafra (southern), and Salibiya/Shagaya/Umm Qudair (central) fields likely feed different distribution zones, so the saturated 90.7 MIGD blendable volume is contingent on the absence of binding zone-isolation bottlenecks. A zone-resolved hydraulic model (out of scope for the present dataset) would identify whether the LP’s optimum is realizable in the operating network or whether additional inter-zone transfer infrastructure is required to capture the full uplift; Section 5.8 replaces that coarse test with the documented nine-station schedule and finds the degradation is negligible only if wells may be assigned to stations individually; if each field feeds a single station, the realizable volume decreases to a median 55.08 MIGD, i.e., 39% below the aggregate optimum. The saturated 90.7 MIGD is accordingly an upper bound throughout. Tenth, the TDS constraint is single-parameter (TDS only), and TDS is an acceptability rather than a health-based parameter (Section 4.5), so no reported volume constitutes a potability determination: for the Ca–-dominated Dammam waters, sulfate (WHO esthetic guideline 250 mg/L–500 mg/L) and total hardness can become the operative limit before TDS reaches 1,000 ppm, so the TDS-only threshold yields a water-quality upper bound on blendable volume in addition to the hydraulic-connectivity upper bound, and a major-ion-aware constraint would likely tighten the feasible set. Eleventh, the LP optimizes a short-run operational ceiling and imposes no multi-year aquifer safe-yield constraint; whether sustained 90.70 MIGD abstraction from these largely non-renewable fields is sustainable against recharge and depletion (Al-Zubari, 2003; Al-Eisa, 2020) is out of scope but essential before implementation, and it would enter the model as a per-field annual-abstraction bound (Section 6, Section 5.6). Twelfth, and following from this, the word “sustainable” is used in this article in the operational sense of sustaining delivered supply against a fixed demand, not in the hydrogeological sense of abstraction within safe yield. No aquifer safe-yield estimate, recharge budget, or drawdown trajectory constrains the optimization, and the fields concerned are largely non-renewable (Al-Zubari, 2003). A dispatch schedule that is optimal here could still deplete the resource, and nothing in these results should be read as evidence that the reported abstraction rates are sustainable in that stronger sense.

7 Conclusion

A linear-programming optimization has been presented in this study, benchmarked against a sorted-by-salinity greedy baseline and a sensitivity sweep, for evaluating the supply-security consequences of rehabilitating legacy brackish-water wells in a desalination-dependent arid-state setting. Applied to Kuwait’s 393-well analytical sample across the five main production fields (Shagaya A-E, Salibiya, Umm Qudair, Wafra, and Atraf), the framework quantifies that current operations support 62.24 MIGD of brackish blending, that mechanical rehabilitation alone increases this to 90.70 MIGD, and that subsequent rehabilitation scenarios (S2–S4) deliver no additional volume because the aggregate pumping-station capacity of 90.7 MIGD becomes the binding constraint. Three qualifications belong in this sentence rather than in a limitations list. The model resolves wells individually but represents the distribution side as a single pooled capacity, so it is a well-resolved aggregate-capacity screening model, not a network-resolved optimization, and it contains no hydraulics. Its optimum is consequently an upper bound: with each field constrained to feed one of the nine documented pumping stations, the realizable median decreases to 55.08 MIGD, 39% below the pooled figure. In addition, the 1,000-ppm bound is an operational TDS acceptability limit (GSO 149), not a health-based potability criterion, so all volumes reported are TDS-feasible upper bounds rather than certified potable supply. The S0S3 factor of 1.46 (a 45.7% increase in dispatched brackish volume, not a water-use-efficiency ratio) increases the total theoretical seawater-desalination displacement to 90.70 MIGD at S3, of which 28.46 MIGD is the increment attributable to rehabilitation, and the remaining 62.24 MIGD is already displaced at baseline; the realized displacement is bounded below this theoretical ceiling by cogeneration dispatch flexibility in Kuwait’s MSF/SWRO fleet, which the present LP does not model. The central planning implication is that brackish-well rehabilitation, on its own, cannot unlock further blending-side displacement beyond the pumping-saturation point; distribution-side capacity must be co-scoped with upstream investment. This conclusion is the basis-independent core of the analysis: explicit zone-partition and standby-reserve stress tests (Section 6, Section 5.1) show that well availability never becomes the binding constraint; a downstream limit (firm pumping or the TDS threshold once the reserve is credited) always binds first, so the LP’s own deliverable is best read as the TDS-feasible, lexicographically-unique dispatch portfolio rather than the saturated volume, which a one-line capacity comparison already implies. Caution is warranted, since the binding-constraint finding rests on an aggregate-scalar abstraction of pumping capacity: the proximate physical bottleneck at the most-constrained station is not identified by the present LP and would require the well-to-station connectivity record, the one dataset whose absence most limits this study. Restricting connectivity does not, however, threaten the direction of the finding: it makes the distribution-side bind harder in 100% of station-resolved solutions. The policy lever is, therefore, co-investigation of distribution-side capacity, with pumping being the leading hypothesis, rather than a pre-committed pumping-only investment. Three candidate bottlenecks merit priority diagnosis: (i) pump-motor capacity at the highest-throughput stations on the Salibiya/Umm Qudair/Shagaya central corridor; (ii) head loss in the longest brackish-water transmission pipelines (notably the Atraf-to-central-zone link); and (iii) tank refill rates at the largest 579 MIGD of connected ground reservoirs, where high-frequency inflow throttling could limit dispatchable volume independently of the well or pump constraints. A two-model salinity benchmark shows that depth and age alone predict well-head salinity weakly , whereas a gradient-boosted model that adds producing-horizon and field features reaches , identifying hydrostratigraphy, not single-well covariates, as the predictive signal. Under field-held-out validation, however, both models fall below an intercept-only baseline ( and ), showing that the apparent skill is between-field interpolation and not transferable hydrogeochemical prediction. Neither is accurate enough to feed the hard TDS threshold, so measured well-head salinity is used directly in the LP. The methodology is aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goal 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) targets 6.4 and 6.5; what can be transferred to other arid-state utilities is the diagnostic (benchmark firm distribution-side throughput against rehabilitated rated well capacity prior to sequencing investment) rather than Kuwait’s specific binding-constraint value, which must be re-derived from each utility’s pumping and demand topology.
